analysis.one_liner: Gives dollar-for-dollar tax credits for donations that pay for private school scholarships.
analysis.headline: The bill got no committee vote and no floor vote; it was introduced with 54 cosponsors, all Republicans, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new federal tax credit covering 100% of donations to nonprofit scholarship organizations, capped at $10 billion a year nationwide. Those organizations would hand out scholarships for elementary and secondary school tuition, including at private and religious schools, to students from households earning up to 300% of their area's median income. The bill would also make those scholarships tax-free and bar any government from controlling the scholarship organizations or the private schools receiving the money.
analysis.who_benefits: Families earning up to 300% of their area's median income who want to send their children to private or religious schools would get scholarship help. Private and religious schools would gain a new stream of tuition money. Donors would get a credit that fully reimburses every donated dollar, up to the greater of 10% of their income or $2,000 for individuals and 5% of taxable income for corporations.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a tax credit equal to the full amount of donations to scholarship-granting organizations — up to the greater of 10% of adjusted gross income or $2,000 for individuals, and up to 5% of taxable income for corporations [S3].
Sets a $10 billion annual cap on the credits, with $1 billion split equally among the states and the rest available nationwide on a first-come, first-served basis [S3].
Scholarships would go to students from households earning no more than 300% of the area median gross income who are eligible to enroll in a public school [S2].
Scholarship amounts used for elementary and secondary education would be excluded from the student's taxable income [S2].

The bill bars any federal, state, or local government from controlling scholarship-granting organizations or private and religious schools, and protects the use of scholarships at faith-based schools [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear up to $10 billion a year in lost revenue, because every donated dollar is credited back against taxes owed. Public school districts would lose funding as enrolled students left for private schools with scholarship money. High-income donors with large tax bills would capture most of the credit, since there is no income limit on who can claim it.

drawbacks.text: Because the credit reimburses donors dollar-for-dollar, a donor with enough tax liability gives at no net cost — effectively redirecting federal tax revenue to the private school of their choice, and the bill sets no income limit on donors [S3].

The 300%-of-median-income cap reaches well into middle- and upper-middle-income households, and the bill requires scholarships to prioritize students who already received one the prior year and their siblings, which limits openings for new lower-income students [S3].

The bill prohibits any government control over the scholarship organizations and the private schools receiving funds, leaving public money flowing with limited public accountability, though it does require annual independent audits and caps administrative overhead at 10% [S3].
Public schools lose per-pupil funding when students leave with scholarships, spreading the cost across the students who remain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Families who want private school options would get real help, and that benefit is genuine. But the design is hard to defend as written: donors are made whole on every dollar, the richest donors can capture the largest credits, up to $10 billion a year would be drained from federal revenue, and the bill deliberately blocks oversight of the organizations and schools that would receive the money. A narrower income cap for students and for donors, with standard accountability rules, would have made the tradeoff far more balanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Labor Committee in June 2022, neither ever took a vote on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Walorski (R-IN) introduced the bill on June 16, 2022 with 10 original cosponsors; it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Labor Committee the same day [S5].
Rep. Walorski died in August 2022, and on September 28, 2022 Rep. Adrian Smith (R-NE) took over as first sponsor so that cosponsors could continue being added [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public school funding and the federal treasury were spared up to $10 billion a year in new tax credits flowing to private schools and fully reimbursed donors. Families hoping for private school scholarships, and the schools and scholarship organizations that would have received the money, gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 54 cosponsors and all 11 original sponsors were Republicans; not a single Democrat signed on, and the bill died in committees chaired by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would open a federally funded tuition stream of up to $10 billion a year to private and religious schools while barring any government control over them. Public schools would lose per-pupil funding as scholarship students left, and taxpayers would fund the credits.

The bill would create a permanent class of 501(c)(3) intermediaries as the sole channel for the credits, letting each keep up to 10% of receipts for administration while prohibiting any government control over how they operate.

A dollar-for-dollar credit with no donor income limit means large donors and corporations (up to 5% of taxable income) can redirect money they would otherwise owe in taxes to private school scholarships they choose, at no net cost to themselves.

Every student who leaves with a scholarship takes per-pupil funding away from the public school community. The bill explicitly protects scholarship use at private and religious schools while offering no comparable support to the public schools losing those students.
